# Code review iteration

Full review of lifeosm/telemost at commit `11f4498 2023-04-18` (history: an `init: clone from go-service at c582be5` plus one gitignore tweak — the tree is a near-pristine copy of the octomation/go-service template). Reviewed: all 21 hand-written and generated Go files (`cmd/`, `internal/`, `api/rpc/v1/`, `static.go`, `tools/`), module files, `.golangci.yml`, `.goreleaser.yml`, Dockerfiles, deploy configs, buf configs, docs stack, and all GitHub workflows/actions. Angle: real defects first, then idiomaticity against 2026-era Go, then toolchain currency. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were ignored as offline backlog dumps. No previous files existed in `.github/reviews/`, so all findings below are new.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Commit message shell injection in the notify composite action

Anchor: `.github/actions/notify/action.yml:26-53` (payload interpolated at line 30).

```yaml
run: |
  if [ '${{ github.event.head_commit.message != null }}' == 'true' ]
  then
    (cat <<-message
  txt=${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}
  message
  ) | head -1 >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
```

`${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}` is expanded by the Actions runner *before* bash parses the script, and the heredoc delimiter is unquoted, so the body still undergoes command substitution. Two attack paths: a commit message containing `$(...)`/backticks executes inside the heredoc, and a message containing a line equal to `message` terminates the heredoc early, turning the remainder into plain shell commands. This is the textbook untrusted-input injection GitHub Security Lab warns about. It is reachable in practice: `ci.yml:127-144` runs `notify` on every push to `main`, and a squash-merge of an external PR puts the attacker-controlled PR title/body into `head_commit.message`. The job has `SLACK_WEBHOOK` in scope and a prior `actions/checkout` with default credential persistence, so both the webhook and the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` are exfiltratable. `github.event.inputs.reason` (line 38) has the same shape but requires write access to trigger.

**Fix.** Never interpolate event payloads into `run:` scripts. Pass them through `env:` (`env: { MSG: ${{ github.event.head_commit.message }} }`) and use `printf 'txt=%s\n' "${MSG%%$'\n'*}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"`. Apply the same to `reason` and `workflow_run.name`. Consider `persist-credentials: false` on checkouts in notify-only jobs.

## 2. Config unmarshal silently overrides the host flag

Anchor: `internal/command/client.go:43` and `internal/command/server.go:138`.

```go
flags.StringVar(&cnf.Server.Connect.Address, "host", "", "remote rpc host")
```

Cobra parses flags *before* running hooks, and the root's `PersistentPreRunE` (`client.go:32-38`, `server.go:40-46`) then executes `v.Unmarshal(cnf)`, decoding the config file over the whole `Service` struct. Since the shipped `config.toml` defines `server.connect.address`, the value the user passed via `--host` is clobbered every time: `client --host 1.2.3.4:8890 hello world` silently talks to `127.0.0.1:8890`. The flag only works when the config file happens to omit the key — the exact inverse of the expected precedence (flag > config > default), and it fails without any diagnostic. As a bonus, the flag is named `host` but actually carries a `host:port` address.

**Fix.** Bind the flag into viper instead of writing to the struct directly: `v.BindPFlag("server.connect.address", flags.Lookup("host"))` before `Unmarshal`, so viper applies its documented precedence. Alternatively, apply the flag value after `Unmarshal` when `flags.Changed("host")` is true. Rename to `--address` (or accept a URL) while at it.

## 3. Release pipeline still targets the upstream template repository

Anchor: `.goreleaser.yml:138-141`, plus `go.mod:1`, `buf.gen.yaml:6`, `api/rpc/buf.yaml:3`, `Dockerfile:6`, `deploy/docker-compose.yml:5`, `README.md` throughout.

```yaml
release:
  github:
    owner: octomation
    name: go-service
```

The template's `run init my.new/service` step was never executed. Consequences go beyond cosmetics: the module is still `go.octolab.org/template/service` (a vanity path owned by another project, so `go install` of this repo's forks collides with the real template); goreleaser is configured to create releases on `octomation/go-service`, push images to `ghcr.io/octomation/go-service`, and open PRs against `octolab/homebrew-tap` — pushing a `v*` tag here with a broadly-scoped `GORELEASER_TOKEN` would attempt to publish artifacts to a *different* repository; `deploy/docker-compose.yml` pulls the upstream image rather than anything built from this code; and the README, docs site, badges, and Docker OCI labels all describe go-service, not telemost. In its current state the repo cannot be released at all and misleads every reader about what it is.

**Fix.** Do the rename pass before any other modernization: module path (`go mod edit -module`), import rewrites, `.goreleaser.yml` owner/name/images/brew, both Dockerfiles' labels, compose image, buf module name, README/badges/docs, `config.toml` service name. Grep for `octomation`, `go-service`, and `template/service` until clean.

## 4. Toolchain and inventory frozen in late 2023

Anchor: `go.mod:3` (`go 1.21`), representative of the whole inventory.

Everything dates to the 2023‑Q4 snapshot of the template and much of it is past end-of-life in mid‑2026:

- **Go**: `go 1.21` directive (EOL since early 2025; current stable is the 1.26 line). CI matrix tests 1.20/1.21 (`ci.yml:61-64`); builder image `golang:1.21-alpine` (`deploy/Dockerfile:1`).
- **Linting**: `golangci-lint v1.55.2` (`tools/go.mod:11`) with a v1 config — `.golangci.yml` uses the removed v2 schema keys (`linters.fast`), lists `typecheck` (not a linter anymore), and enables `exportloopref`, which was deprecated and deleted after Go 1.22's loopvar change; `Makefile:206` additionally force-enables `looppointer`, obsolete for the same reason. `golangci-lint-action@v3.7.0` (`ci.yml:52`) predates the v2 linter entirely.
- **Deprecated deps**: `github.com/golang/mock v1.6.0` (`go.mod:10`) — archived June 2023, superseded by `go.uber.org/mock`; `github.com/twitchtv/twirp v8.1.3+incompatible` — the `+incompatible` marker means it is consumed outside module semantics; `go.uber.org/atomic` era indirects pinned by an old `go.octolab.org`.
- **Actions**: `codecov/codecov-action@v3.1.4` (`ci.yml:124`) — the v3 uploader was shut down; v5 with token/OIDC is current. `goreleaser-action@v5` with a v1 goreleaser config (`brews.folder`, no `version: 2`) will not run on current goreleaser. Everything else (`checkout@v4.1.1`, `setup-go@v5.0.0`, `setup-node@v4.0.1`, `upload-artifact@v4.0.0`) is multiple majors/minors behind, which means dependabot PRs have not been merged since 2023.
- **Codegen**: `buf v1.28` with `version: v1` configs (`api/rpc/buf.yaml:1`, `buf.gen.yaml:1`) — buf v2 changed both file schemas and managed-mode syntax; generated stubs are from `protoc-gen-go v1.31`.
- **Security tooling**: `govulncheck` is in `tools/tools.go:18` and `Makefile:148`, but CI (`ci.yml:78-85`) never runs `go-deps-check`, so vulnerability scanning exists on paper only. No CodeQL either (README lists it as "coming soon" since 2023).
- **Docs**: Next.js ^14 / Nextra ^2 (`docs/package.json:10-11`) — Nextra 4 requires the App Router and Next 15; Node 20 in `cd.docs.yml:39` exits maintenance in 2026. `deploy/docker-compose.yml:1` still carries the obsolete `version: '3'` key.

**Fix.** One migration pass, in dependency order: (1) bump `go` directive to 1.25+, drop the 1.20/1.21 matrix, update `golang:*-alpine` builder; (2) `golangci-lint migrate` to the v2 config, drop exportloopref/looppointer, bump the action to the current major; (3) replace `golang/mock` with `go.uber.org/mock`, re-generate mocks; (4) `buf config migrate` to v2 schemas and regenerate stubs with current plugins; (5) `goreleaser migrate` to `version: 2` config plus `goreleaser-action@v6+`; (6) codecov-action v5, current checkout/setup-* majors; (7) add a `govulncheck` CI job (`make go-deps-check`) and enable CodeQL; (8) rebuild or retire the Nextra docs site. Dependabot config already exists — the real fix is merging what it opens.

## 5. Connect server ignores IsEnabled and falls back to port 80

Anchor: `internal/command/server.go:118-128`.

```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
path, handler := v1connect.NewGreeterServiceHandler(new(server.Connect))
mux.Handle(path, handler)
srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:    cnf.Connect.Address,
    Handler: h2c.NewHandler(mux, new(http2.Server)),
}
```

Twirp, gRPC, gateway, and profile listeners are each guarded by `cnf.X.IsEnabled()` (lines 63, 75, 86, 107), but the Connect server starts unconditionally. If `server.connect.address` is absent from the config, `http.Server.Addr == ""` makes `ListenAndServe` bind `:http` — port 80 on all interfaces — which either fails with a permission error (printed and ignored, see finding 6) or, in a container running as root, silently exposes the service on an unintended public port. The config type explicitly models "disabled" as an empty address (`internal/config/service.go:45-47`), so this violates the module's own contract.

**Fix.** Wrap the Connect block in `if cnf.Connect.IsEnabled() { ... }` like the other protocols, and fail fast with a clear error if *no* protocol ends up enabled.

## 6. Listener failures in goroutines are printed and forgotten

Anchor: `internal/command/server.go:67-73` (twirp), `82-85` (gRPC), `98-104` (gateway), `109-115` (profile), `125-128` (connect).

```go
go func() {
    cmd.Println("twirp server starts listening", cnf.Twirp.BaseURL())
    cmd.Println("twirp server status:", http.ListenAndServe(
        cnf.Twirp.Address,
        mux,
    ))
}()
```

Every server runs in a bare goroutine whose terminal error is passed to `cmd.Println` and dropped. If a port is already taken or the bind address is invalid, the process logs one line and keeps running as a healthy-looking zombie: `run` still blocks on the termination signal, the exit code is 0, and an orchestrator's restart policy never kicks in. There is no readiness signal distinguishing "all five listeners up" from "everything failed". Today's idiom is an `errgroup.Group` (or Go 1.25+ `sync.WaitGroup.Go`) where any `Serve` error cancels the group context and propagates to `RunE`'s return value.

**Fix.** Create each `net.Listener` synchronously (fail fast on bind errors), then run the serve loops under `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` with a shared context: `g.Go(func() error { return srv.Serve(ln) })`, and return `g.Wait()` from `RunE` so a dead listener terminates the process with a non-zero exit code.

## 7. Graceful shutdown covers one of five servers and has no deadline

Anchor: `internal/command/server.go:129-134`.

```go
err := sync.Termination().Wait(cmd.Context())
if errors.Is(err, sync.ErrSignalTrapped) {
    cmd.Println("shutting down rpc server:", srv.Shutdown(cmd.Context()))
    return nil
}
```

On SIGINT/SIGTERM only the Connect `http.Server` is drained. The twirp, gateway, and profile servers (started via package-level `http.ListenAndServe`, which returns an unreachable `*http.Server`) and the gRPC server (`srv.Serve`, never `GracefulStop`) are killed mid-request when the process exits. Worse, `srv.Shutdown(cmd.Context())` is called with the still-alive root context: `Shutdown` without a deadline waits for *all* active connections to finish, so a single hung client blocks termination forever — Kubernetes will eventually SIGKILL the pod, defeating the graceful path entirely.

**Fix.** Keep references to every `*http.Server` and the `*grpc.Server`; on signal, run `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)` and shut all of them down concurrently (`srv.Shutdown(ctx)` for HTTP, `GracefulStop` raced against the same deadline for gRPC). This composes naturally with the errgroup structure from finding 6.

## 8. pprof bound to all interfaces and published by the deployment image

Anchor: `deploy/config.toml:11-13`, with `deploy/Dockerfile:30` (`EXPOSE 3360`), `deploy/docker-compose.yml:7` (`'3360:3360'`), and `internal/command/server.go:6` + `107-116`.

```toml
[server.profile]
address = "0.0.0.0:3360"
```

The blank import `_ "net/http/pprof"` registers the profiler on `http.DefaultServeMux`, and the profile listener serves `http.DefaultServeMux` verbatim (`server.go:108`). The dev config binds it to loopback, but the config baked into the container binds `0.0.0.0:3360`, and compose publishes that port to the host. Public pprof leaks heap contents, command line, and symbol tables, and CPU/trace endpoints are a trivial DoS lever. Serving `DefaultServeMux` also means any handler another dependency registers globally becomes reachable on this port.

**Fix.** Give the profiler a private `*http.ServeMux` with the `net/http/pprof` handlers registered explicitly, drop the blank import, and do not publish 3360 from the container by default — profiling in production should go through a sidecar, port-forward, or an authenticated path.

## 9. Entry point tests drop argv zero and the success case asserts nothing

Anchor: `cmd/server/main_test.go:13-25` and the identical `cmd/client/main_test.go:13-25`.

```go
t.Run("success", func(t *testing.T) {
    exit = func(code int) { assert.Equal(t, 0, code) }
    stderr, stdout = io.Discard, io.Discard
    os.Args = []string{"version"}
    main()
})
```

`os.Args[0]` is the program name; cobra executes `os.Args[1:]`. With `os.Args = []string{"version"}` the root command receives *no* arguments, so it prints help (root has no `Run`) and returns nil — the `version` subcommand under test never executes, `exit` is never called, and the assertion inside it is dead. The subtest passes vacuously and would keep passing if `version` were deleted. The tests also mutate package globals (`exit`, `stderr`, `stdout`, `os.Args`) with no restoration, leaking state into any test that runs later in the binary and ruling out `t.Parallel()`.

**Fix.** Use `os.Args = []string{"server", "version"}` (or refactor `main` into a `run(args []string, out, err io.Writer) int` and test that directly, the current idiom for testable mains). Restore globals with `t.Cleanup`, and make the success case assert on observable output, e.g. capture stdout into a `bytes.Buffer` and check it contains the version string.

## 10. No HTTP server timeouts on any listener

Anchor: `internal/command/server.go:121-124`; also lines 69-72, 100-103, 111-114.

The Connect `http.Server` sets only `Addr` and `Handler`, and the other three HTTP listeners use `http.ListenAndServe`, which cannot carry timeouts at all. Servers without `ReadHeaderTimeout`/`ReadTimeout`/`IdleTimeout` hold connections open indefinitely and are trivially susceptible to Slowloris-style exhaustion; this is exactly what gosec G112/G114 flag, and it is amplified by h2c (line 123), which lets unauthenticated clients open HTTP/2 streams on plaintext.

**Fix.** Construct a `*http.Server` per listener with at minimum `ReadHeaderTimeout` (e.g. 5s) and `IdleTimeout`, replacing the package-level `http.ListenAndServe` calls — which finding 6's restructuring requires anyway.

## 11. Secured flag changes the printed URL but never enables TLS

Anchor: `internal/config/service.go:33-43`, consumed at `internal/command/server.go` (all `BaseURL()` calls) and `internal/command/client.go:57,76`.

```go
scheme := "http://"
if proto.Secured {
    scheme = "https://"
}
```

`Protocol.Secured` only rewrites the scheme in `BaseURL()`. On the server side every listener is plaintext (`ListenAndServe`, h2c, `grpc.NewServer()` without credentials), so setting `secured = true` makes the startup log advertise an `https://` URL that nothing serves. On the client side the same flag flips the dial scheme, so a client whose config says `secured = true` against this server simply fails to connect. A config field that promises transport security without implementing it is an API trap for whoever builds a real service on this skeleton.

**Fix.** Either implement it — `ListenAndServeTLS`/`tls.Config` plus `grpc` server credentials when `Secured` is set, with cert/key paths in `Protocol` — or delete the field until it does something. A comment is not enough; the config format is the template's public contract.

## 12. Duplicated entry points and dead code

Anchor: `cmd/client/main.go:1-65` vs `cmd/server/main.go:1-65`; `internal/server/gateway.go:3-4`; `cmd/client/main.go:30-35`.

The two `main.go` files are byte-identical except for one `command.NewClient`/`NewServer` call — 60 duplicated lines (globals, `init`, `shutdown`) that have already drifted-proofed nothing and will diverge silently. `internal/server/gateway.go` declares an empty, unreferenced `Gateway` struct. And the `init` version stamping produces awkward output: when ldflags are absent, `commit` becomes the literal string `"unknown, mod sum: <sum>"`, while modern practice reads `vcs.revision`/`vcs.time` from `debug.BuildInfo.Settings` (and since Go 1.24 `info.Main.Version` is already git-derived for tagged builds).

**Fix.** Extract a shared `internal/cli.Run(newRoot func(*config.Service) *cobra.Command)` helper so each `main.go` is ~10 lines; delete `internal/server/gateway.go`; derive commit/date from `BuildInfo.Settings` and only fall back to ldflags overrides.
